transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2025-08-27 16:00 PDT
- Duration: 58 minutes
- Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Liam (SE), Ava (SE), Evelyn (Product, Hightide), Carlos (CTO), Priya (ML Eng), Samir (Security)

Summary (auto): Demo of JSON mode and schema-first tool calling. Focus on pilot scoping for order processing assistant: structured actions (create_order, check_inventory, schedule-shipment), guardrails to prevent PII leakage, and runtime fallback to safe model variant.

--- Transcript body ---
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on the account, and with me are Liam and Ava from our SE team. Quick sound check?
[00:08] Evelyn (Hightide): Sounds good, thanks Maya.
[00:10] Carlos: Yep good here.
[00:12] Priya: All set.
[00:15] Maya: Awesome. Goal for today is a compact walkthrough of JSON mode for typed outputs and how you can wire function calls safely to your internal systems — and then scope a short pilot. We'll tailor examples to the order processing use case you mentioned in the questionnaire.
[00:29] Liam (SE): I'll demo the Console runbook and then switch to a live API call showing schema enforcement and a fallback path. Please interrupt with specifics.
[00:37] Evelyn: Great. For context, we're currently using a home-grown webhook orchestrator with a bunch of brittle regex mapping and about 12 different microservices. The pain is inconsistent outputs and a lot of manual error handling.
[00:50] Maya: Right, that matches what you wrote. Quick qualification: are there strict data residency or on-prem constraints?
[00:56] Carlos: We need EU data residency for orders from EU customers, and for certain SKU lines we need on-prem for security reasons. Also the security team will want KMS-backed keys and audit logs.
[01:09] Samir (Security): And SOC 2 readiness — we are already SOC 2 but we'll need to see audit trails and SSO integration.
[01:17] Ava: Totally understood. Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem) supports bring-your-own-KMS and SAML SSO; we can scope which flows require private routing.
[01:27] Priya: On the model side, how does Redwood handle typed outputs when the LLM hallucinates or returns partial JSON?
[01:34] Liam: Good question. In JSON mode you define a schema (we'll demo one for create_order). The runtime enforces parsing and will either reject, attempt auto-correction with a transformation step, or fall back to a secondary safer model variant depending on your policy. There are also structured fallbacks we call 'graceful degradation' where the system returns a validated minimal contract: {"status":"needs_review"} so your orchestration doesn't break.
[01:55] Evelyn: Can you show that? Would like to see a failover.
[01:58] Liam: Sure — switching to screen. 
[02:05] [Screen share noise; brief pause]
[02:12] Liam: Here in the Console runbook you can see the schema editor. For create_order we have fields: order_id (string), items (array of item objects with sku and qty), billing_info (object with tokenized card ref), and customer_consent boolean. You can attach a validation policy: strict, soft, or transform. I'm going to run an example prompt that intentionally omits qty for one item to induce a schema failure.
[02:40] [Typing sounds] 
[02:44] Liam: API call fired.
[02:47] [00:02:48] Speaker transcription artifact: returned output shows missing qty but the runtime applied a transform that inferred qty:1 and returned validated JSON. See the "transform" trace here.
[03:05] Priya: Huh interesting, is that deterministic? We need consistent behavior across retries.
[03:11] Liam: The transform uses deterministic rules if you enable the 'rule-set' option; otherwise transforms are logged and you can set them to require human review. All ops are logged with token-level delta so you can audit what changed.
[03:24] Carlos: What about tool/function calling? We have internal endpoints for inventory and shipping. How do you prevent arbitrary code execution?
[03:33] Ava: Tool calls are mediated by the runtime. You register functions with a contract (name, params schema, allowed response shape) and the console maps them to safe connectors. Calls only execute if the output validates against the function's param schema and passes policy checks like SSO token scopes and network allowlists. We also support a dry-run/validation mode that returns the would-be function call without executing it.
[03:58] Samir: Network allowlists — is that per-function or global? We need per-function network egress control for PCI-related calls.
[04:06] Ava: Per-function. You can also pin which deployment (hosted/dedicated/private) the function is allowed to run from.
[04:14] Evelyn: Can we see an example where the model tries to call an unsupported function and gets rejected?
[04:20] Liam: Yep. I'm going to prompt the assistant to 'refund and ship' which is not an allowed compound action. The runtime will synthesize a potential function call but then policy layer rejects because refund endpoint isn't registered for this model role.
[04:36] [Demo executes] 
[04:40] Liam: Result: assistant suggested calling refund_payment and schedule_shipment; policy denies refund_payment because that function is not bound. The system returned a typed response: {"status":"action_blocked", "reason":"function_not_registered:refund_payment"} and a human readable note.
[04:58] Carlos: Nice. That kind of defensive behavior is exactly what we need.
[05:02] Priya: On latency/cost, what's the hit for strict validation + transforms + function gating? We have tight p95 latency for chat flows.
[05:12] Maya: Great point. Redwood Optimize recommends batching and kv-prefix caching for prompt patterns that are stable. For action calls where latency is critical we can route to a low-latency model variant and enable cache warmups; cost-wise transforms and validation are small CPU overhead compared to generation tokens. We can show model/quantization recommendations based on your token distribution during the pilot.
[05:35] Evelyn: Do you have benchmarks for p95 with validation?
[05:39] Liam: We do — I can share a brief benchmark sheet. Typical p95 for short action calls with validation on A100-equivalent dedicated nodes is ~180-250ms depending on sequence length; hosted can be slightly higher due to multi-tenant scheduling, although dedicated pools with reserved capacity bring it down and give you predictable SLOs.
[05:58] Carlos: Ok. For pilot scope we'll need a predicted cost delta.
[06:03] Maya: We'll include that in the SOW with a sample traffic-profile cost model.
[06:10] [Small cross talk] 
[06:13] Priya: A technical Q: how does the runtime keep KV cache correct when fallback to a secondary model? We worry about context mismatch leading to dupes.
[06:23] Liam: The runtime manages KV cache metadata; when we route to a fallback compatible variant we ensure a cache compatibility shim that maps keys. If the fallback model has different kv encoding we rehydrate from a golden checkpoint. It's engineered to avoid duplication but we'll run targeted benchmarks with your sequence lengths in the pilot.
[06:43] Evelyn: About SSO and audit log integration — Samir will want to see a proof-of-concept for our SIEM.
[06:50] Samir: Yes, we need event-level logs forwarded with context IDs. Can Redwood integrate with our Splunk instance?
[06:56] Ava: Yes, we can forward structured events to Splunk or S3 with customer-managed retention. For Private deployments this lives in your VPC; for hosted we support encrypted log forwarding with customer KMS.
[07:08] Carlos: Any regulatory constraints for EU-resident orders? We need to confirm processing and logs stay in the EU region.
[07:14] Maya: You can pin regions per-route. For EU flows we recommend Private in EU region or Dedicated capacity in the EU with data residency controls. We'll list those options in the SOW.
[07:26] Evelyn: Can we talk about rollback/fallback for model rollouts? We can't have release day degrade.
[07:33] Liam: Console has rollout controls: canary, AB, automatic fallback to previous model if eval metrics degrade. You can tie evals to your prompt set so any quality regression triggers automatic rollback and alerts.
[07:45] Priya: Speaking of evals — can we run quality checks against our labeled prompt set in the pilot?
[07:50] Ava: Yes, Redwood Optimize will run contract checks and surface regressions by schema mismatch rate and semantic quality thresholds.
[07:58] [10min mark: short pause for notes] 
[08:12] Carlos: Budget question — if we go Dedicated for EU and Hosted for US, how does billing work? Single invoice?
[08:20] Maya: We can consolidate billing under one account, but Dedicated contracts have a commit. We'll show a blended pricing option for the pilot in the SOW.
[08:31] Evelyn: Ok, let's scope the pilot. Our desired outcomes: 1) Replace webhook-based create_order flow for 5% of live traffic, 2) Demonstrate safe function calls to inventory and shipping, 3) Prove rollback and audit trail, 4) Measure p95 latency and cost. Target timeline 6 weeks.
[08:50] Maya: Sounds reasonable. Proposed pilot phases: discovery & infra setup (week 0–1), schema mapping and test prompts (week 1–2), integration and dry-run (week 3), live small-traffic run + monitoring (week 4–6), plus wrap and evaluation.
[09:06] Priya: For infra we'll need a small on-prem connector for PCI flows. Is that something you provide?
[09:13] Ava: We provide a connector pattern; for pilot we can set up a SCIM/connector VM in your environment to front PCI calls. If you want full on-prem, that's a Private deployment which we can include as a later phase.
[09:26] Carlos: Do you have recommended schema examples for telemetry and audit tracing?
[09:31] Liam: Yes, we'll share a starter schema bundle: action contract for create_order, check_inventory, schedule_shipment, and a minimal audit event schema.
[09:39] Evelyn: Can Redwood ensure PII removal from logs? We need card tokens not full PANs to leave our network.
[09:45] Ava: We support tokenization and PII scrubbing policies. Tokens can be stored only in customer-managed stores and we can redact fields before logs leave the VPC.
[09:55] Priya: Any limits on function parameter size? Our shipping endpoints expect a fairly complex manifest.
[10:01] Liam: Function params are schema-defined; large payloads are supported but we recommend referencing a manifest id and storing the heavy payload in an object store to keep latency low.
[10:13] Evelyn: Shall we talk about the data collection we need to provide?
[10:17] Maya: Yes: 1) representative prompt set (10–20 examples), 2) sample webhooks and expected responses, 3) network allowlist and SSO metadata, 4) list of functions to map and which require private execution.
[10:30] Carlos: We'll aim to have those by next Friday.
[10:33] Maya: Great. We'll send SOW and a sample runtime config.
[10:36] [Wrap up notes] 
[10:40] Evelyn: Quick question — competitors? We evaluated Anthropic and OpenAI last quarter; Anthropic was strong on safety but lacked schema tooling, OpenAI had tooling but we hit cost issues. Any migration story?
[10:53] Maya: We often migrate customers and can import prompt sets; model routing allows you to use multiple model backends and fallback between them. We'll include a migration checklist.
[11:03] Samir: Ok security will review the SOW.
[11:06] Maya: Thanks everyone. Recap: Redwood to send SOW + pricing, sample schemas, and a proposed pilot timetable. Hightide to send prompt set, list of functions, and network/SSO details. Schedule kickoff the week of 9/8.
[11:20] [End of meeting]

Notes on transcription: Some product names were auto-transcribed as 'Redwood Consol' and 'K V cash' for KV cache. Occasional speaker mislabels near 02:47.
